nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.front: What's the longest-prefix-match rule?
flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

flashcards.front: Default route — what does `0.0.0.0/0` mean?
flashcards.back: It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

flashcards.front: Administrative distance — what is it?
flashcards.back: When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

nodes.title: Automation and IaC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining your servers, networks, databases in version-controlled config files instead of clicking around a console. Pipelines automate the apply step. The combination is what makes cloud reproducible.

flashcards.front: What is the value of declarative IaC?
flashcards.back: You describe the desired state ('I want 3 EC2 instances in this VPC'), the tool figures out how to get there. Reruns are idempotent — applying the same code twice doesn't double anything. State drift (someone clicked in the console) is detected on the next plan/diff.

flashcards.front: Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep — what's different?
flashcards.back: Terraform: cloud-agnostic, HCL syntax, plan/apply workflow, huge ecosystem. CloudFormation: AWS-only, YAML/JSON, native rollback. Bicep: Azure-only, cleaner DSL on top of ARM. Pick the cloud-native tool if you're single-cloud; Terraform if multi-cloud or your team prefers HCL.

flashcards.front: What is a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure?
flashcards.back: Same as for app code: commit → run linter (tflint) → plan / diff → require approval → apply. Production typically has a manual approval gate; lower environments auto-apply. Plan output is reviewed in the PR so a destructive change is caught before merge.

flashcards.front: Why is mutable infrastructure considered an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: Mutable: SSH in, run apt-get, edit configs, server drifts from its template. Two 'identical' servers slowly diverge → snowflakes → 'works on this instance only' bugs. Immutable: bake a fresh AMI / image, replace the running instance, the old one is destroyed. Painful upfront, trivial to roll back, no drift.

nodes.title: CCNP WAN technologies (ENARSI): Key Ideas
nodes.content: ENARSI covers advanced WAN designs. DMVPN is the dominant hub-and-spoke/spoke-to-spoke VPN technology; SD-WAN (Cisco Viptela) is its software-defined successor. The exam tests DMVPN phase behavior, how mGRE and NHRP combine to build dynamic tunnels, and the SD-WAN control-plane component roles.

flashcards.front: DMVPN phases 1, 2, 3 — what changes in each?
flashcards.back: Phase 1: all spoke-to-spoke traffic hair-pins through the hub — hub is the single mGRE anchor, spokes never communicate directly. Phase 2: spokes learn each other's real IPs via NHRP and build dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels — but summarization breaks because the hub can't summarize more-specific spoke routes. Phase 3: adds NHRP redirect — hub redirects spokes to talk directly, full summarization preserved at the hub, best of both worlds.

flashcards.front: mGRE + NHRP — how do they create a dynamic tunnel?
flashcards.back: mGRE (multipoint GRE) is a single tunnel interface on the hub that can accept tunnels from many spokes without a dedicated point-to-point config per spoke. NHRP (Next-Hop Resolution Protocol) maps each spoke's private overlay IP to its public underlay IP — it's the 'directory service' of DMVPN. When spoke A wants to reach spoke B, it queries the hub's NHRP server, gets B's public IP, and builds a direct dynamic GRE tunnel.

flashcards.front: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) — what does each control-plane component do?
flashcards.back: vManage: centralized management dashboard — all configuration, monitoring, policy push. vSmart: control-plane controller — distributes routing policies and OMP routes to all vEdge/cEdge devices. vBond: orchestration component — first point of contact for new devices, authenticates them and redirects to vSmart and vManage. vEdge/cEdge: the data-plane devices at each site that establish IPsec tunnels and forward traffic.

flashcards.front: DMVPN vs SD-WAN — when would you still choose DMVPN?
flashcards.back: DMVPN is a pure Cisco IOS feature requiring no additional licensing or cloud controllers — if your existing estate is all IOS/IOS-XE and the WAN is simple, DMVPN is operationally familiar and cost-free to add. SD-WAN is better when you need application-aware routing (prefer a direct internet path for Salesforce), dual-ISP failover with SLA measurement, zero-touch provisioning at scale, or non-Cisco WAN edges. DMVPN is the right answer for 'I have 10 branch offices and a spare IOS router'.

questions.q: A multi-site enterprise wants to: (a) decouple WAN policy from hardware vendor, (b) use multiple transports (MPLS + broadband + LTE) actively, (c) centralise policy (URL filtering, QoS, app routing) via a controller, (d) push intent-based config to branch CPEs. Which technology?
choices: Software-Defined WAN (SD-WAN)
Software-Defined Data Centre — DC concept, not WAN
Software-Defined Storage — storage abstraction, not WAN
Wireless LAN solution — different domain
questions.explanation: SD-WAN (Cisco Viptela/SDWAN, VMware VeloCloud) centralizes WAN control, enables application-aware routing, automatic failover between WAN links, and reduces costs by using broadband/LTE alongside MPLS.

questions.q: Two routers need to encapsulate ANY Layer-3 protocol (IPv4, IPv6, IPX) inside an IP packet to traverse an intermediate network. The encapsulation adds a 4-byte protocol-id header and an outer IP header. The result LOOKS like an IP packet to the intermediate network but transparently carries the inner payload. Which tunnel?
choices: Fibre Channel — storage protocol, not L3 tunnel
An IPsec security protocol — different concern (security, not encapsulation per-se)
GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation)
VLAN extension (VXLAN) — different overlay (L2 over L3)
questions.explanation: GRE (Protocol 47) wraps packets in an IP + GRE header, allowing non-IP protocols or multicast over IP networks. GRE itself provides no encryption — combine with IPSec for secure tunnels. Used in DMVPN and SD-WAN. encapsulates virtually any Layer 3 protocol inside IP packets, creating a virtual point-to-point tunnel between endpoints across IP networks

questions.q: A hub-and-spoke WAN with 500 branch offices needs spoke-to-spoke dynamic tunnels (without the hub in the data path) WITHOUT pre-configuring every spoke pair. The Cisco solution combines GRE multipoint (mGRE), NHRP for next-hop resolution, and IPsec for encryption. What is this technology?
choices: An SD-WAN product — separate product family (Viptela / Catalyst SD-WAN)
DMVPN
A routing protocol — wrong category
A static VPN — DMVPN is dynamic, not static
questions.explanation: DMVPN phases: Phase 1 (hub-and-spoke, all traffic through hub), Phase 2 (spoke-to-spoke direct tunnels, no summarization), Phase 3 (spoke-to-spoke with summarization via NHRP redirect). Reduces hub load.

questions.q: In DMVPN Phase 2 / 3, a SPOKE wants to talk directly to another SPOKE (not via the hub). It needs to discover the other spoke's PUBLIC (NBMA / underlay) IP from the spoke's overlay tunnel IP. The hub maintains a dynamic mapping table; spokes query it on demand. Which protocol?
choices: A VPN encryption protocol — wrong category (IPsec is encryption; NHRP is mapping)
A DHCP alternative — wrong category
A routing protocol — wrong category
NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol)
questions.explanation: In DMVPN, NHRP allows spoke routers to query the hub for the physical (NBMA) address of other spokes, enabling on-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels without pre-configuring all pairs. Hub maintains NHRP database.

questions.q: Cisco SD-WAN's control plane has THREE planes split across three named components: (A) MANAGEMENT (config UI, policy editor, monitoring), (B) CONTROL (computes overlay routes, distributes them to edge routers), (C) ORCHESTRATION (initial onboarding, NAT traversal helper). Which mapping?
choices: All three are legacy SD-WAN components replaced by Cisco Catalyst Center — false; vManage, vSmart, and vBond are the current Cisco SD-WAN control plane architecture

vManage, vSmart, and vBond are three names for the same physical controller that handles management, control plane routing, and orchestration simultaneously — false; they are three distinct functional components
vManage = management plane (GUI/API/config), vSmart = control plane (OMP routing policy), vBond = orchestration plane (authentication/NAT traversal for edge-to-controller connectivity)
vManage, vSmart, and vBond are hardware-only appliances; software implementations are not supported in Cisco SD-WAN deployments — false; all three can run as virtual machines
questions.explanation: SD-WAN planes: Management (vManage: telemetry, templates, policies), Control (vSmart: OMP routes, policy enforcement, key distribution), Data (vEdge/cEdge: IPsec tunnels, forwarding), Orchestration (vBond: initial device onboarding, NAT discovery). API, policy config). vSmart: control plane (OMP routing protocol, policy distribution). vBond: orchestration plane (initial authentication, NAT traversal for WAN edges)

questions.q: A multi-WAN-path enterprise (MPLS + broadband + LTE) wants APPLICATION-aware path choice: VoIP must always take the lowest-jitter path, large file copies the cheapest, web traffic the lowest-latency. The decision is RE-EVALUATED per real-time IP-SLA metric. Which Cisco IWAN feature?
choices: Firewall feature — wrong category
Routing protocol — wrong category
QoS mechanism — wrong category
PfRv3 (Performance Routing)
questions.explanation: PfRv3/IWAN: master controller monitors path performance via IP SLA probes, moves traffic between MPLS/broadband based on policy thresholds per application class. Replaced by Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) which does the same more elegantly.

questions.q: A branch router has a primary WAN to the HQ via MPLS and a backup via internet. PBR routes specific source-IPs via the MPLS path. The team adds IP-SLA probes through the MPLS path with object-tracking: if probes fail, the PBR rule is dynamically disabled and traffic falls back to the default route via internet. Which combination is this?
choices: PBR + IP-SLA object-tracking
A routing protocol — too generic
BGP multihoming — different mechanism
Firewall failover — wrong product
questions.explanation: Example: PBR route-map matches HTTP traffic, sets next-hop to MPLS if SLA probe up, internet if down. 'set ip next-hop verify-availability [IP] [seq] track [obj]'. Multiple next-hops tried in order until verified reachable.

questions.q: A WAN team needs an encrypted tunnel that ALSO carries non-IP protocols (multicast, OSPF Hellos, IPX, NHRP) over the public internet. Standard IPsec TUNNEL mode encrypts unicast IP only and doesn't expose a routable tunnel interface. The solution: wrap traffic in GRE first (provides a tunnel interface + multicast / any-protocol support) and protect GRE with IPsec. Which?
choices: GRE over IPsec
GRE over IPsec and IPsec tunnel-mode identical — false
GRE provides encryption — false; GRE is unencrypted
IPsec supports multicast natively — false; vanilla IPsec doesn't carry multicast
questions.explanation: IPSec transport mode: encrypts payload, original IP header preserved. IPSec tunnel mode: encrypts entire IP packet, new IP header added. GRE+IPSec: GRE creates tunnel interface for routing/multicast, IPSec encrypts GRE packets. Most enterprise VPNs use GRE+IPSec.

nodes.title: CCNP Campus (ENCOR / SD-Access): Key Ideas
nodes.content: ENCOR covers Software-Defined Access as the Cisco campus architecture. SD-Access separates the underlay (traditional routed/switched network) from the overlay (VXLAN tunnels) with LISP as the control plane to track endpoints. Cisco DNA Center is the management plane. These concepts are tested together with questions on fabric roles and endpoint mobility.

flashcards.front: SD-Access three-layer architecture — underlay, overlay, control plane.
flashcards.back: Underlay: traditional IS-IS-routed network of campus switches providing IP connectivity between fabric nodes — fast, simple, stable. Overlay: VXLAN tunnels between fabric edge nodes carry segmented traffic (VNs map to VRFs); endpoints' traffic is encapsulated at the first fabric node they attach to. Control plane: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) on the Map Server tracks where each endpoint is and responds to lookup requests — decouples who an endpoint is (EID) from where it is (RLOC).

flashcards.front: LISP — EID vs RLOC — what is each?
flashcards.back: EID (Endpoint Identifier): the stable IP address of an endpoint — it doesn't change as the device roams the campus. RLOC (Routing Locator): the IP address of the fabric edge (border or edge node) currently hosting the endpoint — this changes when the device moves. The LISP Map Server maintains an EID-to-RLOC mapping database. When fabric node A wants to reach an EID, it queries the Map Server, gets the current RLOC, and sends VXLAN-encapsulated traffic there.

flashcards.front: VXLAN in SD-Access — why use it instead of VLAN?
flashcards.back: VLANs are scoped to a single broadcast domain and don't scale beyond a building or campus floor without complex STP management. VXLAN encapsulates L2 frames in UDP/IP packets, enabling L2 segment extension across an L3 underlay fabric without STP. The 24-bit VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier) supports 16 million segments vs VLAN's 4094 — essential for per-user/per-IoT-device micro-segmentation at campus scale.

flashcards.front: Cisco DNA Center vs traditional Campus Manager — what changed?
flashcards.back: DNA Center is intent-based: you declare a policy ('this user group gets access to these apps') and DNA Center translates it into device configuration across the fabric — no manual CLI per switch. It provides discovery, topology, assurance (real-time health scores), and automation (Day-0 through Day-N provisioning). Traditional Campus Manager required per-device configuration; DNA Center treats the entire fabric as a single managed system with a declarative API.

questions.q: Cisco's campus network architecture uses: VXLAN overlay fabric, LISP for the overlay control plane, ISE for identity-based policy (SGT tags), and DNA Center for orchestration. Endpoints get a scalable group tag (SGT) and policy is enforced uniformly. What is this called?
choices: Cisco SD-Access
A routing protocol — wrong category
Cloud-only solution — false; SD-Access is on-prem campus
A WAN solution — that would be Cisco SD-WAN, separate product
questions.explanation: SD-Access: Underlay (routed access), Overlay (VXLAN/LISP), Policy (ISE+SGT/SGACLs), Management (DNA Center). Virtual Networks (VNs) provide macro-segmentation; Scalable Group Tags (SGTs) provide micro-segmentation.

questions.q: Cisco SD-Access uses a control-plane protocol that separates an endpoint's IDENTITY (Endpoint Identifier, EID) from its LOCATION (Routing Locator, RLOC). When an EID moves to a new RLOC (host mobility), the control plane updates the mapping without changing the IP address. Which protocol?
choices: A security protocol — wrong category
An encryption protocol — wrong category
A routing protocol — partial truth (LISP IS a routing protocol) but the BEST answer is the identity-location separation property
LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
questions.explanation: LISP maps EIDs to RLOCs via a Map-Server/Map-Resolver. When a host moves, only the LISP map changes, not the routing table. In SD-Access, LISP distributes host-to-switch-location mappings across the fabric. IP/MAC) from its location (RLOC — routing locator) — enables mobility without changing routing tables. Used as overlay control plane in Cisco SD-Access

questions.q: Cisco SD-Access uses two complementary segmentation constructs. (A) MACRO segmentation — entire routing domain (VRF-lite-style), separating tenants. (B) MICRO segmentation — 16-bit tag attached to users/devices by ISE; enforcement points compare tags via Cisco TrustSec. Which mapping?
choices: Wireless network types — wrong category
VN (Virtual Network) = macro segmentation (per-tenant routing domain)
VLAN alternatives — partial; SD-Access uses VNs/SGTs that subsume some VLAN roles, but the distinction is macro vs micro segmentation
Security zones — too vague
questions.explanation: SD-Access segmentation: VNs (like VRFs) for isolation between major groups (IoT, Guest, Corp). Within a VN, SGTs (1-65535) tag users/endpoints by role. SGACLs (Cisco TrustSec) enforce which SGTs can communicate.

questions.q: In LISP, every packet to a new EID would normally trigger a Map-Request to the Map Server. Sub-second performance requires caching the EID-to-RLOC binding LOCALLY at the LISP router so subsequent packets to the same destination skip the lookup. What is this?
choices: A BGP route cache — different surface
LISP Map Cache
A routing table entry — different data structure
DNS caching — different surface
questions.explanation: LISP first packet: ITR sends Map-Request to Map-Resolver → Map-Server → responds with RLOC. ITR caches EID→RLOC mapping. Subsequent packets: encapsulate directly using cached RLOC. Map-Cache: show lisp site / show lisp map-cache.

questions.q: Cisco's HIERARCHICAL campus reference design separates roles. The CORE provides high-speed L3 backbone between buildings. The DISTRIBUTION layer aggregates access switches and applies L3 policy. The ACCESS layer attaches end-hosts. In a SMALLER campus a 2-tier 'COLLAPSED CORE' merges core + distribution. Which mapping is correct?
choices: 3-tier always best — context-dependent
Identical — false
2-tier is only small offices — false; small/mid campuses use it routinely
3-tier = Core + Distribution + Access (large
questions.explanation: 3-tier: Core (campus backbone, high-speed, no policy), Distribution (routing, ACL, STP, redundancy per building), Access (PoE, VLANs, 802.1X). 2-tier: eliminate separate core for smaller designs. Modern: spine-leaf replacing 3-tier in many designs.

questions.q: Cisco SD-Access supports two complementary segmentation models. MACRO uses Virtual Networks (VNs/VRFs) to provide COMPLETE ROUTING ISOLATION between large groups (corporate / IoT / guest). MICRO uses Scalable Group Tags (SGTs) inside a VN to control inter-group access without per-VLAN ACLs. Which mapping?
choices: Macro segmentation uses VN/VRF routing tables to provide full Layer-3 isolation between large tenant groups; micro segmentation uses SGTs to enforce per-flow policy within a VN at the fabric edge
Only macro segmentation using VNs is supported in SD-Access — false; SD-Access supports both VN-based macro segmentation for routing isolation and SGT-based micro segmentation within a VN
Micro segmentation requires separate physical hardware to enforce SGT policy independently of the macro segmentation VN routing isolation — false; both run on the same SD-Access fabric nodes
Macro and micro segmentation in SD-Access are different names for the same Virtual Network construct — false; macro uses VRF/VN routing separation while micro uses SGTs for granular per-flow policy
questions.explanation: SD-Access layers: VN (VRF-based, L3 isolation, separate routing table per VN) = macro. SGT (16-bit tag assigned by ISE) = micro. SGACLs: 'permit/deny' between source SGT and destination SGT. Both can coexist — VN isolation + fine-grained role policy within VN.

questions.q: Cisco SD-Access extends to wireless. WLCs run in SD-Access mode, APs operate as 'fabric APs' (FAPs) sending CAPWAP control to the WLC but DATA-PLANE tunnelling directly to the edge node via VXLAN. Wireless clients get an SGT assigned by ISE on auth. Same policy / segmentation applies to wired + wireless. Which describes SD-Access wireless?
choices: Only on new APs — partially; SD-Access does need supported APs but the BEST answer is the architectural one
Legacy WLC-only — false; SD-Access requires SD-Access-capable WLC
Separate wireless product — false; SD-Access integrates wireless natively
SD-Access extends fabric to wireless
questions.explanation: SD-Access wireless: Fabric-enabled WLC, fabric-mode APs (AP acts as VXLAN VTEP or tunnels to fabric edge). Client: connects to SSID → WLC assigns VLAN/VN/SGT via ISE → traffic enters fabric → same policy as wired. Seamless roaming within fabric.

questions.q: A retail enterprise uses its Wi-Fi infrastructure for INDOOR LOCATION SERVICES — tracking connected devices, generating heatmaps, exposing APIs for marketing apps (welcome messages, dwell-time analytics). The service is cloud-based and integrates with WLCs and APs. What's this service?
choices: A security service — different surface
A routing platform — wrong category
Cloud DNS — wrong service
Cisco DNA Spaces (now Spaces)
questions.explanation: DNA Spaces: uses Cisco AP RSSI data for location. REST APIs for app integration. Use cases: retail analytics (dwell time, path analysis), hospital asset tracking, workplace occupancy. Requires Catalyst Center + CMX license or DNA Spaces subscription.

nodes.title: VXLAN and Cisco ACI (CCNP): Key Ideas
nodes.content: VXLAN (Virtual eXtensible LAN) is the data-plane encapsulation protocol used in virtually every modern data center fabric and SD-Access campus. Cisco ACI is the policy-driven SDN fabric built on VXLAN with APIC as the controller. CCNP tests VTEPs, VNIs, the BGP EVPN control plane, and ACI's object model of EPGs and contracts.

flashcards.front: VTEP and VNI — what are they?
flashcards.back: VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint): the device (switch, router, hypervisor vSwitch, or software) that originates and terminates VXLAN encapsulation. VTEPs encapsulate L2 Ethernet frames in UDP/IP (UDP port 4789) and send them across an L3 underlay. VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier): a 24-bit segment ID that identifies the VXLAN segment — 16 million possible VNIs vs VLAN's 4094. VNI is the VXLAN equivalent of the VLAN ID.

flashcards.front: VXLAN vs VLAN — why does VXLAN win in modern data centers?
flashcards.back: VLANs are limited to 4094 IDs, can't stretch across L3 boundaries without complex extensions (OTV), and require STP for loop prevention. VXLAN uses 24-bit VNIs (16M segments), runs over a standard L3 underlay (no STP), scales to thousands of switches, and enables VM/workload mobility across the data center without IP address changes. Multi-tenancy at scale — each tenant gets VNIs, not VLANs.

flashcards.front: BGP EVPN as the VXLAN control plane — what does it do?
flashcards.back: Without a control plane, VTEPs flood unknown unicast/broadcast/multicast (BUM) traffic to all VTEPs to learn MAC-to-VTEP mappings — inefficient at scale. BGP EVPN (RFC 7432) provides a control plane: VTEPs advertise their locally learned MAC/IP bindings as BGP EVPN routes (Type 2 routes). Remote VTEPs learn MAC-to-VTEP mappings via BGP before any data traffic, eliminating flooding. This is 'MAC routing' — applying routing discipline to L2 learning.

flashcards.front: Cisco ACI — APIC, spine, leaf, EPG, contract — how do they relate?
flashcards.back: APIC (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller): the SDN controller cluster that holds the intent-based policy model and pushes config to fabric switches. Spine: L3 backbone switches (no endpoints attach, only leaf-to-leaf connectivity). Leaf: access-layer switches where servers, VMs, and external networks connect. EPG (Endpoint Group): a logical group of endpoints (VMs, bare-metal) with identical policy requirements — replaces VLANs as the segmentation boundary. Contract: the policy that permits or denies traffic between EPGs — EPGs don't talk to each other unless an explicit contract allows it.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: A bank's MPLS WAN already provides privacy + segmentation. The bank ADDITIONALLY needs to encrypt traffic between sites without altering the underlying IP headers (so transit MPLS PE/P routers can still forward by label). The Cisco VPN uses GROUP keys — all members share one key + SA. Which technology?
choices: GETVPN (Group Encrypted Transport VPN)
Remote-access VPN — different shape (per-user tunnels)
Standard site-to-site IPsec — adds new headers and requires per-pair SAs; doesn't fit
DMVPN variant — different shape (overlay tunnels, not in-place encryption)
questions.explanation: GETVPN uses Tunnel-less encryption (preserves original IP headers) via GET VPN with a Key Server (KS) distributing group keys to Group Members (GMs). Traffic encrypted in place on existing MPLS WAN. No tunneling overhead.

questions.q: Cisco's Trustworthy Systems initiative for routers/switches includes: (a) a hardware ROOT OF TRUST stored in a TAm (Tamper-resistant Anchor module) chip, (b) Secure Boot validating signature of each boot stage, (c) Image Signing of IOS, (d) Run-time defences against tampering. What is the goal?
choices: Hardware Root of Trust + Secure Boot +
A routing protocol — wrong category
A firewall product — wrong category
An authentication system — wrong category
questions.explanation: Cisco Trustworthy Systems: TAm/SUDI chips provide hardware identity. Secure Boot verifies IOS code signatures. ACT2 (Anti-Counterfeiting Technology 2) prevents fake hardware. Network operators can verify device authenticity cryptographically. code signing, SUDI (Secure Unique Device Identity) certificates, and TAm (Trust Anchor Module) ensuring Cisco devices boot trusted code and can be cryptographically identified

questions.q: Cisco TrustSec assigns each AUTHENTICATED endpoint a 16-bit GROUP TAG by ISE. Switches and routers carry the tag inline with packets (inline tagging or via SXP). Enforcement is at the egress device — comparing src + dst tags against an access matrix. The model decouples policy from IP / VLAN. What is this tag?
choices: A routing protocol — wrong category
A VPN technology — wrong category
SGT (Scalable Group Tag)
An encryption standard — wrong category
questions.explanation: TrustSec propagation: Inline tagging (hardware support, L2 tag preserved hop-to-hop), SXP (software protocol mapping SGT to IP for non-TrustSec devices). SGACLs enforced at egress switch or ASA/FTD based on source/destination SGT pair.

questions.q: An ISP wants to PREVENT BGP route hijacks (an unrelated AS advertising prefixes it doesn't own). A PKI-based system has prefix-holders CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY sign Route Origin Authorisations (ROAs) declaring 'AS-X is authorised to originate prefix P/24'. Routers validate received BGP updates against the RPKI repository and drop invalid origins. Which system?
choices: A firewall certificate system — wrong category
RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)
A DNS security extension (DNSSEC) — wrong protocol
A routing protocol — RPKI is a security framework over BGP, not a routing protocol itself
questions.explanation: RPKI: prefix owner creates ROA (prefix, origin AS, max prefix length) signed by RIR (ARIN, RIPE). BGP routers validate announcements against RPKI validator — Invalid routes rejected/de-preferred. Critical defense against BGP hijacking (like AS 7007, Pakistan Telecom incidents).

questions.q: A data centre wants WIRE-SPEED HOP-BY-HOP encryption + authentication on every Ethernet link between switches. The encryption is at Layer 2 (after the Ethernet header, before the EtherType payload) so each switch decrypts + re-encrypts at each hop. IEEE 802.1AE defines it. Which standard?
choices: L3 encryption — wrong layer (IPsec is L3)
MAC address security feature — different feature (port-security)
MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE)
Wireless-only — false; MACsec is wired Ethernet
questions.explanation: MACsec: encrypts each Ethernet frame between adjacent devices. Use cases: campus distribution-to-core, switch-to-server links. MKA (MACsec Key Agreement) handles key exchange via 802.1X. Different from IPSec (L3) or TLS (L7) — provides L2 encryption.

questions.q: CDP and LLDP advertise device platform / OS version / IP / port / capabilities to LAN neighbours. An attacker on an unauthorised port can read these advertisements to plan their attack. The MITIGATION is to disable CDP/LLDP on UNTRUSTED (access) ports while keeping them on inter-switch trunks for management visibility. Which describes the risk and mitigation?
choices: Disable on all interfaces always — over-broad; needed on inter-switch links for ops
CDP/LLDP advertise platform / IOS version / IP / port
No risk — false
Only CDP has the risk — false; LLDP advertises the same
questions.explanation: CDP leak: attacker learns switch model (exploitable vulnerabilities), IOS version, management IP. LLDP has same risk. Best practice: 'no cdp enable' + 'no lldp transmit' + 'no lldp receive' on DMZ/external/user-facing ports. Keep enabled on trunk/uplink ports for topology management. IOS version, IP addresses, interface info — valuable for attackers doing network reconnaissance. Mitigation: disable on external-facing interfaces ('no cdp enable' per interface), enable only on trusted internal ports

nodes.title: Network platform fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Platform-level network concepts cover programmability, automation, and the software-defined layers that modern networks — and CCNP exams — build on top of traditional switching and routing.

flashcards.front: Cisco DNA Center — primary role?
flashcards.back: Intent-based networking controller for campus/branch: provisions devices, applies policies, and provides assurance analytics from a single dashboard.

flashcards.front: REST API verbs for CRUD operations?
flashcards.back: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). Responses use HTTP status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found, etc.

flashcards.front: YANG model — what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Defines a vendor-neutral data model for network device configuration and state, used with NETCONF and RESTCONF for structured automation.

flashcards.front: Northbound vs southbound API in an SDN controller?
flashcards.back: Northbound: API the controller exposes to applications (REST/gRPC). Southbound: API the controller uses to program network devices (OpenFlow, NETCONF, RESTCONF).

questions.q: Cisco ships THREE distinct OS lineages. (A) Modular IOS for enterprise routers and switches (ASR, ISR, Cat9k). (B) Carrier-grade high-availability OS for service-provider edge (ASR9k / NCS). (C) Linux-based DC OS for Nexus switches with VDCs and per-process restart. Which mapping is correct?
choices: IOS-XE = enterprise modular IOS (ASR/ISR)
Three names for the same software — false
Different protocols — false; all three are device OSes
Legacy versions — false; all three are current
questions.explanation: IOS-XE: modular architecture (SPA/SIP separation), enterprise-grade. IOS-XR: microkernel, in-service software upgrade (ISSU), massive scale, 32-bit process separation. NX-OS: Linux-based, programmable, feature-rich for data center.

questions.q: A Cisco chassis with redundant Route Processors (RPs) maintains forwarding during an RP failover. The ACTIVE RP continuously syncs control-plane state (RIB, FIB, adjacencies, protocol state) to the STANDBY RP. On failover, the standby takes over in milliseconds with NO route flap (the FIB stays programmed). What's this feature pair?
choices: An HSRP enhancement — wrong product (HSRP is first-hop redundancy)
A spanning-tree feature — wrong layer
A backup routing protocol — wrong category
NSF + SSO
questions.explanation: Without NSF/SSO: RP failure = routing restart = traffic loss during convergence. With SSO: standby RP fully synchronized, sub-second failover. With NSF: keeps forwarding during reconvergence. OSPF/BGP/EIGRP-aware NSF helpers exist.

questions.q: Cisco offers three multi-chassis switching constructs. (A) Stackwise — two or more access switches stack via physical cables, behave as one virtual switch (Cat 3750/3850/9300). (B) VSS — TWO Cat 6500/4500 chassis act as one logical switch (legacy DC core). (C) vPC — two Nexus switches present a port-channel jointly to a downstream device, but each has its OWN control plane. Which mapping?
choices: Identical — false
VSS needs special modules — partially true (VS-S720-10G) but not the distinction asked
Stackwise = physical-cable single-virtual-switch
Only Nexus stacks — false
questions.explanation: Stackwise: physical ring cable, 80Gbps backplane, 9 switches max, single management IP. VSS: active/standby supervisor, full mesh between chassis, geographic separation possible. vPC: most complex, fully independent management, data center focused.

questions.q: A network operator upgrades the IOS on a core router WITHOUT a maintenance window. Traffic must continue forwarding; routing protocol adjacencies must NOT flap. The operation requires: (a) redundant supervisors with NSF / SSO, (b) compatible OS versions side-by-side (forward+backward compat), (c) ISSU-aware feature image. What's this called?
choices: In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU)
Regular software update — would require maintenance window
Requires maintenance window — false; ISSU avoids it
ASR-only — false; available on many Cisco platforms
questions.explanation: ISSU process: standby RP upgraded first, switchover (SSO), active RP upgraded, switchover back. Throughout: NSF maintains forwarding, SSO maintains protocol states. Requires: SSO configured, NSF for OSPF/BGP/EIGRP, ISSU-capable hardware, compatible versions.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: Cisco IOS marks packets with a QoS field in the IP header. The MODERN marker uses 6 BITS of the IP TOS / Traffic Class byte (giving 64 possible values, e.g., EF, AF41, CS6, DSCP 46). The LEGACY marker used 3 bits (8 values, IP Precedence). The modern marker is a superset that includes the legacy via Class Selector codepoints. Which statement is correct?
choices: DSCP and IP Precedence use DIFFERENT header fields — false; both use the same TOS / Traffic Class byte
DSCP only marks voice — false; DSCP marks all classes (voice, video, bulk, etc.)
DSCP (RFC 2474) = 6 bits, 64 values
IP Precedence is modern, DSCP is legacy — reversed
questions.explanation: DSCP uses 6 bits of the original ToS byte (IP header), allowing 64 PHB (Per-Hop Behavior) values. Expedited Forwarding (EF/46): low latency for voice. Assured Forwarding (AF): guaranteed minimum bandwidth. CS (Class Selector): backward compat with IP Precedence.

questions.q: A QoS configuration deals with congestion ALMOST FILLING the queue. Tail-drop (drop the next arrival when queue is full) causes TCP global synchronisation. A smarter mechanism drops packets RANDOMLY before the queue fills, with drop probability weighted by their DSCP / IP-Precedence marking. Which mechanism?
choices: WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection)
QoS classification — separate task (matching traffic)
QoS marking — separate task (DSCP setting)
QoS policing — token-bucket rate enforcement, drops or re-marks excess; different from RED-style avoidance
questions.explanation: WRED profiles: min-threshold, max-threshold, drop probability. Between min/max: random drops proportional to congestion. Above max: drop all. Different profiles per DSCP class. Prevents tail-drop TCP sync where all TCP flows simultaneously reduce rate.

questions.q: A multicast deployment uses an explicit-join model: receivers register with a designated Rendezvous Point (RP) by sending PIM Joins toward it; sources register with the RP and traffic is forwarded down the shared tree (or via SPT switchover). The protocol is independent of the unicast routing protocol — relies on whatever IGP is present. Which mode?
choices: PIM Sparse Mode
QoS mechanism — wrong concept
PIM Dense Mode — flood-and-prune (the OPPOSITE of explicit-join sparse)
Unicast routing protocol — multicast PIM is for multicast, not unicast
questions.explanation: PIM-SM (RFC 7761) builds shared trees via RP and source trees (SPT). Receivers join via IGMP; PIM Join messages travel toward RP/source. Cisco uses Auto-RP or PIM BSR for RP discovery. SSM (Source Specific Multicast) avoids RP entirely. assumes receivers are sparse. Uses a Rendezvous Point (RP) for initial source/receiver discovery; direct source trees built after RPT path established

questions.q: A multicast deployment wants Rendezvous Point HA without complex RP-failover protocols. Multiple physical RPs are configured with the SAME anycast IP advertised from each location. Sources / receivers find the topologically CLOSEST RP via unicast routing. MSDP redistributes source-active info between RPs. Which feature?
choices: A multicast load balancer — too vague
PIM Anycast RP
Unicast routing feature — that's the mechanism, not the multicast feature name
A PIM version — anycast RP is a configuration, not a protocol version
questions.explanation: Anycast RP: multiple PEs advertise same RP address. Sources/receivers join nearest RP. RPs share source state via MSDP (SA messages) or native Anycast RP (PIM Register). Provides RP redundancy and load distribution without VRRP.

questions.q: A service provider offers customers an Ethernet-like LAN service across multiple geographic sites — ALL customer sites act as if connected to one giant L2 switch. Bridge MAC learning happens across the SP's MPLS / IP transport. Which technology?
choices: Site-to-site IPsec — L3 tunnel, not multipoint L2 bridging
VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service)
Layer-3 VPN — L3 service, not L2 bridging
DMVPN — Cisco hub-and-spoke overlay, not multipoint L2 SP service
questions.explanation: VPLS creates a distributed virtual switch across provider MPLS network. All customer sites appear in same L2 domain. Uses PWs (pseudowires) between PE routers. Replaced increasingly by EVPN which provides the same service more efficiently.

questions.q: Service-provider MPLS L3VPN delivers separate routing tables per customer. Each customer's routes are kept distinct via (a) VRFs on PE routers, (b) MP-BGP carrying VPNv4 prefixes (= RD-prefix + RT), (c) MPLS labels in the data plane for tenant-segregated forwarding. Which is correct?
choices: Customer-managed firewall segmentation — each customer deploys their own firewall to segment traffic; the SP network carries the traffic transparently without per-customer VRFs
Customer VRFs (Virtual Routing and Forwarding instances) on PE routers plus MP-BGP with the VPNv4 address family to carry customer routes with Route Distinguishers across the SP MPLS core
Customer-managed GRE tunnels — customers build point-to-point GRE tunnels over the SP network for separation; the SP does not maintain per-customer routing tables

A generic MPLS tunneling protocol that labels packets for switching — MPLS provides the forwarding but does not itself create separate customer routing tables; VRFs + MP-BGP provide the L3VPN separation
questions.explanation: MPLS L3VPN: CE connects to PE (eBGP/static/OSPF). PE imports routes into VRF, redistributes into MP-BGP VPNv4. RT import/export controls which VPNs receive which routes. P routers: no customer routes, only label forwarding. Two labels: outer (LSP) + inner (VRF).

questions.q: An NetFlow capability records IP flows. Standard NetFlow has FIXED key fields (5-tuple). The MODERN evolution lets the operator DEFINE: which keys to use (e.g., source-IP + ToS only), which non-key fields to collect (interfaces, byte counts, TCP flags, AS path), and which exporters / collectors to send to — per cache. Which feature?
choices: Flexible NetFlow
An IOS version — wrong category
QoS mechanism — wrong category
Routing protocol — wrong category
questions.explanation: Flexible NetFlow: flow record (define keys + non-key fields), flow exporter (IPFIX/NetFlow v9 to collector), flow monitor (combines record + exporter, applied to interface). Collectors: SolarWinds, PRTG, ntopng, ELK stack.

questions.q: An ops team wants ACTIVE measurement of network performance: send synthetic ICMP / UDP / HTTP / DNS / VoIP probes, record one-way and round-trip latency / jitter / loss, and alert / failover based on thresholds. The probes originate from IOS itself. Which Cisco IOS feature?
choices: A routing protocol — wrong category
A QoS tool — wrong category
IP SLA
An SLA document — that's a contract, not a feature
questions.explanation: IP SLA: 'ip sla 1' define operation (icmp-echo, udp-jitter). 'ip sla schedule'. 'show ip sla statistics'. Track SLA with 'track 1 ip sla 1 reachability' → use in routing: 'ip route ... track 1' (floating static based on reachability).
